claim: A cognitive-diagnostic framework combining multidimensional IRT with a hand-built item-ability association matrix (Q-matrix) decomposes LLM benchmark performance into fine-grained ability dimensions (35-dim for math, 27 for physics, 58 for chemistry, 12 for computer science).
stance_target: feasibility of Q-matrix + IRT decomposition for LLM capability structure
scope_conditions: 41 LLMs across math, physics, chemistry, computer science benchmarks; whole-question granularity, not per-requirement code sub-tasks
quoted_support: The framework constructs domain-specific ability taxonomies grounded in cognitive theory and domain knowledge; for mathematics, this yields a 35-dimensional taxonomy. An item-ability association matrix (Q-matrix) encodes which fine-grained abilities each benchmark item (question) engages.

claim: The ability-decomposition framework predicts model performance on unseen benchmark items with AUC 0.80-0.89 within-benchmark and 0.77-0.86 cross-benchmark, substantially exceeding trivial baselines.
stance_target: predictive validity of latent-ability decomposition for held-out item performance
quoted_support: our approach demonstrates strong criterion validity, consistent ability estimates across benchmarks, and accurate prediction of unseen items with AUC ranging from 0.80 to 0.89 within benchmarks and from 0.77 to 0.86 across benchmarks, substantially exceeding trivial baselines.

claim: Prior IRT adaptations for LLM evaluation treat benchmark items as atomic units and lack explicit item-to-fine-grained-ability mappings, limiting them to coarse-grained performance summaries.
stance_target: gap in existing IRT-for-LLM literature that a Q-matrix/mIRT approach fills
scope_conditions: general LLM evaluation literature as of 2025-2026
quoted_support: these adaptations treat benchmark items as atomic units and lack explicit mappings between items and the fine-grained abilities they engage. Consequently, they remain confined to coarse-grained performance summaries and cannot support ability-level diagnosis for targeted improvement or task-aligned selection.
